_title_note: SERIES AMENDMENT, ruled by Jodie 5 Aug 2026 and written into PP-STANDARDS §1a: when an episode belongs to a series we have named, the SERIES NAME carries the title and the ARTICLE'S OWN HEADLINE becomes the byline. So this is 'Squeeze Those Odds! — Part 2', not 'Each-Way Betting Forever!'. Her reason: it makes the two episodes visibly a pair, which is worth more than fidelity to a headline nobody searches for. The source agrees — PP runs both 1988 Dedman articles under different headlines and this one links back to 'squeeze-those-odds-part-1-19880206', which is EP15's source exactly. The bang still sits on the NAME, then the em dash, then the part (2 Aug rule, unchanged).
_shape_note: TWO MOVEMENTS, and the article's own hinge sentence divides them. (1) WHAT A PLACE BET IS WORTH — the theory, from 'three chances but a quarter of the odds' to the five-live-chances case. (2) WHAT TO DO ABOUT IT — the split, and the professionals' favourite bet. The hinge is Roger's own 'Let's consider a race (with eight or more runners) in which the favourite (F) is quoted at evens', which is where he stops deriving and starts advising. The midroll sits ON that seam, at beat 15.

beats.line: OPEN (original framing — the only invented prose besides the seams). An each-way bet is not one bet with a safety net; it is TWO bets sold in one transaction, and once you price them separately you can see which half is the value. Roger Dedman credited, nineteen eighty-eight.
Many people refuse ever to bet each-way, arguing that in the long run you are further ahead sticking to straight-out bets.
The main argument: it is poor value. Three chances of collecting instead of one, but only a QUARTER of the odds. Under eight starters, a third — first or second only.
It may SEEM you should get a third with eight or more runners. In fact the correct odds lie somewhere between a third and a quarter.
The hypothetical: nine evenly matched runners. Probability of winning one in nine — odds of eight to one.
Place chance is three times that: one in three, or two to one. So a quarter of the odds is theoretically CORRECT. Roger's own arithmetic, and it is the pivot of the whole piece.
For eight, slightly less than a quarter. As the field grows, increasingly MORE than a quarter — but never as high as a third.
Twenty-four starters at Flemington: win odds twenty-three to one should give place odds of seven to one. Very nearly one third.
But evenly matched fields do not occur, and we are concerned with practical punting. The theory can be modified — ON-COURSE, where the punter's advantage over the T A B punter is greatest.
The realistic case: FIVE horses with a winning chance, the rest at long odds. Each one in five, quoted four to one. The outsiders are the bookie's margin.

THE VALUE BEAT. Ignore the outsiders and the place chance is three in five — six to four ON. But backing him each way at four to one gets you EVEN MONEY for the place. The place portion is better value than the win portion.
So why not just back the place? Because you won't be offered evens. Five horses at evens brings a place bookie two hundred and fifty when he needs three hundred. He can only afford six to four on.
Despite that, four to one each way is usually obtainable if you shop around — four to one the field is an open race, and plenty of bookmakers will be operating each way.

Win-only signs go up when the favourite is odds-on. An each-way sign means cramped odds about everything else — but in the circumstances that can still beat a straight-out bet. The further the favourite is into the red, the more pronounced the advantage.
MIDROLL — pool line L6, copied verbatim from docs/midroll-line-pool.md (16 mod 10 = 6). Never written, never paraphrased. Sits ON the article's own hinge, between the theory and the advice.
The setup. Favourite at evens; your selection better value at five to one; best each way is four to one; place bookies have it at two to one on. What SHOULD the place odds be? Six to four on.
Which is better — five to one straight-out, or four to one each way? Eight dollars at fives gives forty. Instead: ten dollars each way at fours. And you can think of that as TWO SEPARATE BETS.

THE SPLIT, and the centre of the episode. Twenty dollars re-read as eight for the win — still five to one — and twelve for the place to win ten, which is six to five ON when the correct odds are six to four on. So four to one each way beats five to one straight-out.
Even seven to two each way is a fair bet. The extra twenty-six dollars invested, for a place profit of seventeen fifty, is almost exactly six to four on.

Each-way under four to one: most punters won't. A winning bet at three to one each way LOSES money if the horse runs second or third. Others go further — six to one or longer, or eight to one or longer.
Short-sighted, says Roger. Several professionals go to the OPPOSITE extreme — making a speciality of backing selected favourites each way at two to one and even shorter.
The situation: the favourite can win, and there is ONE logical danger, or at most two. Usually restricted class at provincial meetings, occasionally in the city.

The dangers around four to one, everything else double figures. The favourite at two to one each way is two to one ON for the place, when you think it a near certainty to place. So: four hundred to two hundred each way. Places only — loses a hundred. Wins — five hundred profit.
Occasionally it runs out of a place and that is four hundred gone — but the extra profits more than compensate in the long run. And the same reasoning applies to a ten dollar bet, or less.

Getting set is not the problem. Each-way bookmakers may have the dangers at seven to two — but so few punters want the favourite each way that it is unlikely to be shorter with the win-and-place than the win-only bookies.

OUTRO wind-down (original prose, within the approved shape). It was never one bet with a safety net; the only question is whether each half is worth its share. The half everybody ignores is quite often the half that is paying.

OUTRO standing: free e-book with Roger's tables, link below the video; the LOCKED responsible-gambling line, word for word; warm sign-off, re-voiced per the pattern and never repeated verbatim from a previous episode.

_beats_note: TWENTY-SEVEN BEATS. The count is the ARTICLE'S, not a target: its argument is a chain of short arithmetic steps and each one needs its own breath. Four paragraph pairs were MERGED back after a first pass ran to thirty-one, because that pass was splitting more finely than Roger does — the merge changed paragraph breaks only, and render_ready reports the identical 1,876 words either side of it. Beats 1, 26 and 27 are the seams (opening, wind-down, standing outro) and beat 15 is the midroll; every other beat is Roger's own sentences, lightly tidied for the ear.
_framing_note: FOURTEEN WIDE OF TWENTY-SEVEN. Every panel-push card beat is WIDE, without exception — a panel-push card needs WIDE for its WHOLE window so Gordon can glide aside into the freed third; on an MCU the card lands on his face, which is the EP11 failure. MCU is kept for the seams (1, 26, 27), the midroll (15, per the standard: Gordon on camera), and the four beats that are Roger reasoning rather than Roger demonstrating (4, 7, 14, 24). ⚠️ EP15 ran 14 WIDE of 24 and Jodie has NOT yet given a framing ruling on the finished cut — see the run log. This episode was framed by the same rule EP15 was corrected INTO, not by copying its ratio.

cards.cue: a quarter of the odds is theoretically correct

cards.headline: WHY A QUARTER IS FAIR
cards.detail: The two odds resolve side by side, then the quarter relationship draws between them.

trace.1 in 9: The theoretical probability of any given horse's winning is 1/9, i.e. odds of 8-1.
trace.1 in 3: The probability that that horse runs a place is three times 1/9, i.e. 1/3, or odds of 2-1.
